subject.title: Sometime During Eternity . . .
subject.author: Lawrence Ferlinghetti
subject.text:
Sometime during eternity
                                                       some guys show up   
and one of them
                      who shows up real late
                                                       is a kind of carpenter   
      from some square-type place
                                              like Galilee
          and he starts wailing
                                          and claiming he is hip
            to who made heaven
                                       and earth
                                                      and that the cat
                   who really laid it on us
                                                 is his Dad

          And moreover
             he adds
                         It's all writ down
                                              on some scroll-type parchments   
          which some henchmen
                  leave lying around the Dead Sea somewheres   
                a long time ago
                                       and which you won't even find   
         for a coupla thousand years or so
                                                 or at least for
      nineteen hundred and fortyseven
                                                      of them
                            to be exact
                                             and even then
         nobody really believes them
                                                   or me
                                                            for that matter
          You're hot
                         they tell him
          And they cool him

          They stretch him on the Tree to cool

                         And everybody after that
                                                               is always making models   
                                          of this Tree
                                                          with Him hung up   
          and always crooning His name
                                     and calling Him to come down   
                                 and sit in
                                                 on their combo
                           as if he is the king cat
                                                            who's got to blow   
                      or they can't quite make it

                      Only he don't come down
                                                         from His Tree
          Him just hang there
                                       on His Tree
          looking real Petered out
                                          and real cool
                                                             and also
                   according to a roundup
                                                    of late world news   
             from the usual unreliable sources
                                                               real dead

title: He Joked About the Cross the Year He Beat an Obscenity Charge
standfirst: Lawrence Ferlinghetti published this jive-talk crucifixion the year after he stood trial, and won, for publishing Allen Ginsberg's Howl. He had also walked through Nagasaki twelve years earlier, six weeks after the bomb, and never once told that story for a laugh.

sections.heading: The Alibi Built Into the Last Line
sections.body:
The poem ends on a hedge, not a verdict. Eleven sentences of chatty, put-on gospel — a hip nobody who shows up late, gets called hot, gets stretched out to cool — arrive at their final piece of news only through a source the poem has just finished discrediting: he is, "according to a roundup / of late world news / from the usual unreliable sources / real dead." Not dead. Reportedly dead, filed by the same unreliable channel that, two stanzas earlier, took nineteen hundred and forty-seven years to get around to publishing its own scripture.

That qualifier does real work, and it does not always land. Jerry Cimino, who runs the Beat Museum in San Francisco, has written about first meeting this poem in eighth grade in 1968, fresh out of Catholic school, and hearing it flatly as a "God is dead" statement — only understanding later that the "unreliable sources" line was the poem's actual argument, not a throwaway joke. A poem built to sound like it is settling something is, read closely, doing the opposite: refusing to settle anything at all.

sections.heading: A Gospel Translated Into Hepcat
sections.body:
The method is translation, not mockery for its own sake. Christ becomes "a kind of carpenter / from some square-type place / like Galilee"; God becomes "the cat / who really laid it on us" and, a line later, flatly "his Dad"; the crucifixion becomes a scene where the crowd tells him "You're hot" and "they cool him." Even the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls, nine years before Ferlinghetti wrote this, gets folded into the bit — "some henchmen / leave lying around the Dead Sea somewheres," found only after the poem's own comic arithmetic of "nineteen hundred and fortyseven" years.

The poem first appeared in Ferlinghetti's second collection, A Coney Island of the Mind, published by New Directions in 1958. It went on to sell roughly a million copies and, by one standard account, became the best-selling book published by any living American poet in the second half of the twentieth century. A private joke about scripture, told in slang built to expire, turned out to have an audience most poets never get.

sections.heading: The City He Never Made Into a Bit
sections.body:
Ferlinghetti had earned the right to be flip about death, if anyone had. He served in the U.S. Navy through the Second World War, commanding a submarine chaser off the Normandy beaches in 1944. The following September, a twenty-six-year-old lieutenant by then, he walked through Nagasaki roughly six weeks after the atomic bomb had leveled it — a landscape of flattened, pulverized buildings, and human remains fused into ordinary objects that had survived the blast. Accounts differ on the specific object: one description has him finding a teacup with a human finger still curled around its handle; another describes a cup with flesh and bone fused directly into the porcelain. Either way, he kept it, reportedly for the rest of his long life.

The experience made him, by his own later account, a lifelong pacifist where he had previously had no real politics at all. In 1962 he helped found the San Francisco chapter of Veterans For Peace, marching, unofficially at first, at the tail of the city's official Veterans Day parade. Nothing in the record suggests he ever told the Nagasaki story in the register he used for a resurrection: no jive, no punchline, no unreliable sources to hide behind.

sections.heading: A Publisher Fresh Off His Own Trial
sections.body:
The timing of the book is not incidental. Ferlinghetti ran City Lights, the San Francisco bookstore and press that had published Allen Ginsberg's Howl and Other Poems in 1956. On June 3, 1957, San Francisco police arrested Ferlinghetti and his shop clerk, Shigeyoshi Murao, for selling an obscene book, months after U.S. Customs had already tried and failed to block copies at the border. The case went to trial that summer, with nine literary experts testifying on the poem's behalf, and on October 3, 1957, Judge Clayton W. Horn ruled in Ferlinghetti's favor. His written opinion held that Howl was not "without redeeming social importance," reading its two halves as, respectively, a nightmare vision and an indictment of a culture wrecked by materialism, conformity and the drift toward war. Horn added a broader principle that reads almost like a licence: "An author should be real in treating his subject and be allowed to express his thoughts and ideas in his own words."

A Coney Island of the Mind followed in 1958, from the same press, the same city, the same man — a book that opens a poem about the crucifixion with a man who "starts wailing" and God as "the cat." A publisher who had just spent a summer defending someone else's right to blaspheme in whatever words he chose went straight home and used the freedom on his own material.

sections.heading: Christ as the Cat Who's Got to Blow
sections.body:
The poem's slang is not generic beatnik costume; it is specifically musicians' slang, and Ferlinghetti was, that same year, reading his own poems over a live rhythm section. In spring 1957, poets including Ferlinghetti and Kenneth Rexroth began performing at the Cellar, a former Chinese restaurant turned nightclub in North Beach, with jazz musicians improvising underneath the reading — an early, deliberate fusion of the two forms that Ferlinghetti kept using afterward: two other poems from the same 1958 collection, "I Am Waiting" and "Junkman's Obbligato," were written expressly for jazz accompaniment.

Read against that practice, one image in this poem stops being incidental. After the crucifixion, Ferlinghetti writes, people keep "calling Him to come down / and sit in / on their combo / as if he is the king cat / who's got to blow." Christ is recast, specifically, as a musician being begged out of retirement for one more set. He never comes down. The line only works as a joke if the reader already understands sitting in on a combo as an honor a musician can refuse — which is exactly the audience Ferlinghetti had, by then, spent a season performing for in a basement club, live, over a horn section.

sections.heading: The Label He Spent Decades Refusing
sections.body:
For all that this poem now reads as a stock artifact of the Beat era — the slang, the irreverence, the jazz-club provenance — Ferlinghetti resisted being filed there. "Don't call me a Beat," he said, flatly. "I never was a Beat poet." He had, after all, come to poetry by way of a doctorate from the Sorbonne and a scholarly dissertation on the image of the city in modern verse, not by way of the road or the commune; the persona in this poem, chatty and slangy and pretending not to have read a book, was a costume he could put on and remove.

That is, perhaps, the sharpest thing about "Sometime During Eternity": it was written by a man capable of holding both registers at once, sometimes within the same year — the wisecracking jive of a resurrection nobody can quite confirm, and the flat, unfunny record of a city he had once walked through that no one needed a hedge to describe as real dead.
